newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, waiting for op, a shadow of former self.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, waiting for op, a shadow of former self.

text.p: The world has had two images of Russian President Boris Yeltsin since February 15, when he launched a successful bid to win a second term in office.

The first Yeltsin shook hands with supporters, defended his policies at packed public meetings across Russia and danced for the crowds during a hectic election campaign accompanied by blanket coverage from compliant media.

The second Yeltsin was an altogther different man -- he received small numbers of invited guests, spoke cautiously at stage-managed television appearances and barely stepped outside the Kremlin or government rest homes.

It was only after 10 weeks of infrequent meetings, media speculation and frenzied denials from aides that anything serious was wrong that Yeltsin, 65, admitted publically that he needed an operation on his heart.
Eight days later he went into hospital for checks, and the one-time workaholic now spends just two or three hours a day working on papers.
Doctors say it will take at least six weeks to prepare him for a bypass operation to improve the flow of blood to his heart. But he has a good chance of making a full recovery.

"The president is a courageous man," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference on Friday. "He has taken the news that he has to limit his workload very staunchly and is getting ready for surgery, as advised by his doctors."

Checks on the president's schedule and media reports of his activities since the end of June show around a dozen meetings, most of them with premier Viktor Chernomyrdin in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow.
The president also met chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and U.S. vice-President Al Gore. But security boss Alexander Lebed had to wait for an interview.

"He (Yeltsin) communicates with a limited circle of people of which I am not a part," Lebed, who has suggested that the president should delegate power during his illness, told Izvestia newspaper last week.

Yeltsin has also appeared on television a dozen times, but he often seemed to walk stiffly or have difficulty working out what to say. Television footage, released by the Kremlin, sometimes carried no sound at all.
Before the second round, a tireless Yeltsin had half a dozen televised engagements a day on campaign trips across Russia. Aides said he slept for four or five hours a night.

But Yeltsin retreated to the sanatorium between the two rounds of Russia's presidential election. His press office initially said he was tired and had lost his voice and dismissed reports that he was in hospital.

"You should understand better than us that somebody would use such rumours to play the (financial) market," press service head Igor Ignatyev said on July 2, one day before the runoff vote. "Somebody is making money on it."
The news that the president needed a heart operation broke a long tradition of silence about the health of Kremlin leaders.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said Yeltsin should resign and failed presidential candidate Vladimir Zhirinovsky suggested that long periods away from the Kremlin could violate Russian labour law.

"I see it in the light of the labour code," the flamboyant ultra-nationalist told a news conference last week. "If one is unable to work for three months, one gets disability and gets sacked. That is valid for all employees in Russia -- whether it's a street cleaner or a president."
